19714-with-frederick-the-great-a-story-o:
G. A. Henty wrote adventure novels that taught boys history through war. With Frederick the Great tells the Seven Years' War. Henty opens by weighing the war's stakes. Had Prussia been crushed, he argues, Protestantism might have vanished from Germany. The whole course of later events would have changed. He adds that the war mattered nearly as much to Britain.

Henty's formula put a young hero beside great events. Readers learned campaigns while following invented lives. Frederick's Prussia, fighting larger coalitions, suited that formula well. Henty wrote dozens of such novels, all confident and brisk. This one shows his method at its clearest. History first, adventure as the delivery truck.
20173-the-romance-of-golden-star:
George Griffith wrote The Romance of Golden Star, a tale of lost Inca treasure. A sleeper who looks like an Inca lord draws the heroes' awe. If he woke, he could tell how that lost wonderland truly was. He could answer riddles, disprove lies, and reveal hidden treasure at once.

Griffith wrote bold tales of empire, war, and hidden gold for eager readers. Peru's past gives this romance its temples, tombs, and perilous quests. Greed and wonder pull the party deep into old Inca lands. Readers get lost-world adventure in the rich, pulpy style of its day.
20207-under-wellington-s-command-a-tale-:
G. A. Henty wrote Under Wellington's Command, a tale of the Peninsular War. Henty admits one book cannot hold that whole war in outline. To try would make a history, not a tale, he tells readers. His earlier tale had closed with the passage of the Douro.

That crossing drove the French from Portugal in a bold stroke. Now the tale takes up the thread where it left off. Young heroes serve under Wellington through sieges and hard marches in Spain. Readers get Henty's usual mix of true campaigns and boys' bravery.
20354-jack-of-both-sides-the-story-of-a-:
Jack of Both Sides tells the story of a school war at Brincliffe. New boys were lawful game at many schools of the era. But these new boys were also day-pupils, a great grievance there. Only last term had the first day-boy been admitted at all.

Wiseacres prophesied that Jim Bacon was the thin end of the wedge. Boarders and day boys line up as two camps in the war. School stories turn such splits into battles of honor and wit. Readers get a lively tale of loyalty, prejudice, and boyish combat.
20404-all-round-the-year:
E. Nesbit, best known for her children's novels, also wrote verse, and All Round the Year moves through the seasons in poems. The poems mark the turning months with flowers, weather, and city streets. Many were written with young readers in mind.

One poem follows a busy, dusty wind along cruel streets. The wind reaches the heart of violets and robs them of their sweets. Nesbit then turns the image on people: cold kindness met in the street can blight a poor heart the same way. The book mixes charm with such sharp little truths.
20724-the-man-with-the-broken-ear:
Edmond About, a French writer famed for wit, wrote the fantastic novel sold in English as The Man with the Broken Ear. The letters in the text speak to Leon, far from home, and hint at illness and longing at home. A strange find soon turns that homesick talk into a much odder tale.

About mixes science talk, satire, and adventure in one fast story. The broken ear of the title points to a dried human relic with a past of its own. Readers who like early science fiction with a sharp comic edge will find a brief, strange, and lively book here.
20729-at-the-point-of-the-bayonet-a-tale:
G. A. Henty wrote boys' adventure tales set inside real wars, and his Mahratta War story is a clear case. The text calls the fall of the Mahratta power one of the most stirring pages in Britain's Indian campaigns. Those campaigns ran from Clive's day to a firm British rule across the peninsula.

A young hero moves through marches, sieges, and fights as great powers clash around him. Henty packs in period detail about camps, arms, and Indian courts. Modern readers can see both the pull of the adventure form and the imperial views of Henty's age, held side by side on the page.
20849-the-big-brother-a-story-of-indian-:
Summer 1813 opens The Big Brother, George Cary Eggleston's tale of Indian war. Creek bands in Alabama and Mississippi had turned hostile that year. Quiet days of peace, Eggleston warns, make such times hard for later minds to grasp.

A big brother's care for the young gives the tale its name and heart. Frontier homes, alarms, and fights test that bond to the edge. Eggleston knew war at first hand from his own service. His tale mixes boyhood adventure with a veteran's sense of what frontier fear truly felt like, day by day.
21046-story-hour-readings-seventh-year:
Each great race keeps a heritage of story and song, E. C. Hartwell tells seventh-year readers. Hero songs, origin tales, moral fables, and pure fancy all share that store. Story Hour Readings gathers such goods for the seventh school year.

Hartwell chose tales to hold pupils in the last grammar years with worthy matter. Myths, ballads, history tales, and nature pieces fill the reader in turns. Notes help teachers draw out each tale's point in class talk. The book shows how schools once fed young minds on the world's old stories, held to be a birthright of every child.
21136-for-fortune-and-glory-a-story-of-t:
Lewis Hough opens at Harton, a boarding school much like Eton, before sending his heroes to the Soudan War. A former employee, an Egyptian, has stolen a will from a Dublin solicitor, along with an earlier version of it. Because of that theft, a family lost its money when an Eastern bank failed before the war.

Two story lines run side by side: the hunt for the stolen wills and the fighting in the Soudan. School slang and cricket give the early chapters their flavour. In the end the wills are tracked down and justice is done for the estate, while the war scenes carry their own weight.
21201-journal-of-a-voyage-to-brazil-and-:
Maria Graham sailed to Brazil and lived there through parts of 1821, 1822, and 1823, during Brazil's break from Portugal. Her journal, published in London in 1824, records the voyage and the residence. She admits in her preface that she cut many pages on public and private events before printing.

Graham writes honestly rather than with perfect impartiality, which she calls no virtue in some cases. She gathers facts that reached Europe one by one and records how events felt on the spot. The result is a sharp English traveller's picture of a new empire forming, its court, ports, and daily life.
21242-on-the-irrawaddy-a-story-of-the-fi:
G. A. Henty's preface warns that few of Britain's little wars killed so many, in proportion, as the first expedition to Burma. Stanley, his young hero, sails up the Irrawaddy as war breaks out. Chapter titles carry him from a new career to capture, a ruined temple, and service on the staff.

Burmese general Bandoola, the fight for the great pagoda, and the advance on Donabew all appear. Stanley is carried off and rescued along the way. Henty notes how Burmese forces stripped the country of boats and food, pinning the British in Rangoon through one wet season. Victory humbles Burma's pride by the end.
21326-the-black-bar:
HMS Nautilus patrols the west coast of Africa in George Manville Fenn's tale. She intercepts American and Portuguese slave ships bound to buy human cargoes for the Atlantic crossing. Two midshipmen serve aboard her, and Mark Vandean is the hero. The black bar of the title is a heraldic mark of shame in a family's arms.

Fenn drops Mark into one dreadful situation after another, solved often by something unexpected. The patrol setting shows British sea power used against the slave trade in African waters. Equatorial calms, glistening seas, and sudden action alternate as the Nautilus works her station and Mark's ancestry shadows his name.
21374-tention-a-story-of-boy-life-during:
Private Penton Gray, called Pen, wakes wounded in a ravine after a volley. In George Manville Fenn's Peninsular War tale, the boy bugler Punch lies hurt beside him. British troops are near, but French soldiers hold the ground where the boys lie. They must heal in hiding and then find their regiment.

Helpers along the way include the deposed king of Spain himself. Once back, the commanding officer learns that Pen has the education of an officer. He uses Pen's knowledge of the mountains to lead the troops against the French rear. The attack routs the French, and Private Gray is promoted to officer rank on the strength of it.
21398-black-bruin-the-biography-of-a-bea:
Black Bruin, Clarence Hawkes's 1908 life story of a bear, follows one animal from cubhood in the deep woods. Hawkes wrote many such lives of wild creatures, among them a beaver's tale. Charles Copeland's drawings show the bear's world of forest, stream, and mountain.

The tale opens with theft, a chase, and a wild baby bear learning to live. Bruin meets hunters, traps, and a panther, and learns the ways of his kind. Hawkes tells it as a life, not a pet's romp, with real risk at each turn. Young readers who love true-feeling animal stories will find a full one here.
22100-slavery-and-four-years-of-war:
Joseph Warren Keifer, a Union general and later Speaker of the House, published Slavery and Four Years of War in 1900. His subtitle promises a political history of slavery and a personal history of the war of 1861 to 1865. Keifer opens with slavery's long past, older than written history itself. He traces it from barbaric times into the American republic he helped save.

The second half turns to his own service with Ohio troops. Keifer fought in the Shenandoah Valley and rose to command a corps. His verdicts on generals and campaigns carry a participant's weight. The book joins two subjects that shaped his life: the sin he opposed and the war he fought.
22464-the-last-of-the-chiefs-a-story-of-:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Last of the Chiefs, a story of the Great Sioux War. Its young hero, Richard Howard, faces a terrible problem at the start. He feels no fear on his own account, Altsheler writes.

A boy in years, Richard is a man in self-reliance. His boyhood on an Illinois farm taught him wood and field. Where prairies slope up to forest, he learned their ways. He is full of courage, strength, and resource for the trail. The story sets him amid the Sioux wars of the plains. Altsheler's frontier tales were favorites with young readers. This one mixes history, danger, and a capable boy hero.
22537-mr-dooley-in-peace-and-in-war:
Mr. Dooley in Peace and in War, dated 1898, collects Finley Peter Dunne's famous sketches. Mr. Dooley is a Chicago bartender who comments on the news. His pub stands in Archey Road, an Irish-American neighborhood.

There one can see wakes and christenings in American dress. Marriages and funerals of the old country appear modified by usage. The Banshee has been heard many times in Archey Road itself. On All Saints' Eve, pookies play tricks in cabbage gardens there. Dooley's brogue carries sharp satire on politics and war. The Spanish-American War fills many of these pieces with bite. Readers get American humor that presidents themselves read and quoted.
22666-the-rainy-day-railroad-war:
Holman Day wrote The Rainy Day Railroad War, a novel of labor and timber country in Maine. The catalog record gives no year. Day, a Maine journalist and novelist, made his name with stories of lumber camps, ward politics, and the men who ran both.

In the sample, a troubled young man named Parker protests the broken promises made to the work crews. The food was to be free of weevils and spoilage. Instead the Italian laborers went half starved and did poor work, while their padrone pocketed the money meant to feed them. Crooked middlemen, hungry crews, and a railroad pushing through wet country set the conflict. Day writes with a reporter's ear for camps and a reformer's anger at graft.
22755-the-adventures-of-the-little-woman:
The Adventures of the Little Woman, Her Dog and the Pedlar is a children's chapbook in verse, with pictures, of the kind once sold for pennies. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its pages mix a comic rhyme story with short moral poems spelled out in syllables for beginning readers.

In the tale, a dog stops barking and the little woman cries out in comic surprise that now she knows who she is. The companion poem teaches that whatever brawls may disturb the street, peace should reign at home. Birds in their little nests agree, it sings, and it is a shameful sight when children of one family fall out and fight. Such chapbooks were the first books many children ever owned.
22816-the-adventures-of-buster-bear:
Buster Bear wakes up hungry in the Green Forest in Thornton Burgess's 1916 animal story book for children. He yawns on his bed of leaves, watches the first sunbeams chase out the shadows, and shakes himself awake. From that slow morning start, his day of wandering and mischief begins.

Each short chapter puts Buster among his neighbors, the rabbits, squirrels, and other forest folk Burgess made famous. The tales teach natural history through talk and teasing rather than lessons. Buster is strong, a bit greedy, and often outwitted, which keeps him likable. Generations of children met American wildlife through books like this one, and the gentle humor still carries the stories.
23036-dave-darrin-after-the-mine-layers-:
H. Irving Hancock lists the action in Dave Darrin After the Mine Layers. The chapter headings promise a renewed grapple, a mine-sweeper's daily round, and a captain lost overboard. Later comes the hour of despair, a vanishing destroyer, the meeting of searchlights, a cowboy Dane, and a German prisoner who talks at last.

Darrin, Hancock's naval cadet grown officer, fights the Great War at sea in this entry of a long boys' series. Mine warfare made unglamorous, deadly work, and the book sells it as high adventure. The pace is relentless, the patriotism open. Readers meet the war as American boys of 1919 were invited to imagine it, dangerous, technical, and winnable by nerve.
23241-my-daily-meditation-for-the-circli:
J. H. Jowett's My Daily Meditation for the Circling Year, published in 1914, offers a short devotional reading for each day. One entry reflects on Abraham. Abram began his journey, Jowett notes, with no knowledge of where he would end up. He obeyed a noble impulse without seeing what would come of it.

He took one step, without demanding a view of the road ahead. That, for Jowett, is faith: to do what God asks today, and leave the outcome to Him. Readers get brief, plain meditations meant for daily use across a full year.
23263-the-fugitives-the-tyrant-queen-of-:
The Fugitives is a tale of the tyrant queen of Madagascar. Its author warns readers, honestly, that he has shifted time and place a little. He has also mixed his characters and their deeds somewhat, to suit the conditions of his tale and the story he wants to tell.

Even so, he says he strove to avoid exaggeration. His aim was a true picture of affairs at the period treated. The island itself draws his highest praise, as one of the most interesting and progressive in the world. Readers get adventure under a feared queen, with a storyteller who admits where invention begins.
358-the-scarlet-car:
Richard Harding Davis tells four linked motoring tales in this brisk volume, all set among rich young New Yorkers and their cars. A Harvard-Yale game trip opens the book, and each later tale turns on a bold drive, a rescue, or a chase. The scarlet car itself becomes a mark of speed, nerve, and luck.

In one tale friends break a man out of jail by road; in another they foil kidnappers; in a third they race to save a romance. Davis writes fast dialogue and bright road scenes, with little time for doubt. The stories capture an early motoring age, when a car could still feel like a daring new machine.
566-the-history-of-the-thirty-years-war:
Friedrich Schiller narrates the Thirty Years' War in this history, translated by A. J. W. Morrison. Schiller traces the Reformation's effects, the revolt of Matthias, the Bohemian rising, and the clash of Union and League, with lucidity and impartial judgment. His preface praises his own gift for history as well as drama.

Chapters move from emperors and electors to armies and treaties, showing how faith and power tore Europe apart. Schiller writes as a dramatist turned historian, keen on character and cause. The work endures as a classic popular history, clear, grave, and humane.
605-pellucidar:
Edgar Rice Burroughs returns to the hollow Earth in this sequel to At the Earth's Core. A letter from Algiers lures the narrator from lion hunting in Africa back to Pellucidar, where David Innes fights Hooja's cutthroats, cave prisons, and raids. Chapters race from lost wanderings to conquest and peace.

Burroughs writes at his usual gallop, with chutes, captures, kidnappings, and escapes. The inner world's eternal sun and strange beasts frame each peril. The book charms as a brisk continuation, where a modern hero must win a stone-age world by nerve and friendship.
793-aeroplanes-and-dirigibles-of-war:
Frederick A. Talbot wrote this account of flying machines in war, at a time when their use was still new and much debated. He traces the dirigible balloon and the aeroplane from early trials to their first service, weighing what each could do for scouting, bombing, and naval work. Theories, he notes, outran proof for years.

Talbot gathers reports from the first air war, with details on types, crews, and raids. His prose is clear and factual, aimed at readers who want to grasp a fast-changing art. The book is a valuable record of how war in the air looked while it was still being invented, before later histories tidied the story.
92-tarzan-and-the-jewels-of-opar:
Gold from the lost city of Opar draws Tarzan back to its vaults, and trouble follows. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar opens with Belgian and Arab rivals on the road to the city. The priestess La still guards the altar of the Flaming God.

Tarzan steals jewels, loses his reason, and leads the apes again as a beast. Werper the Belgian steals the treasure in turn, and Jane Clayton faces capture and peril. The novel weaves two thefts and a rescue into one chase. Opar's gold keeps pulling Tarzan between man and ape.
a-short-history-of-the-great-war:
A. F. Pollard, professor of English history in the University of London, published A Short History of the Great War in 1920, as the title page records. In twenty chapters with nineteen maps he tells the whole First World War in one volume, from the breach of the peace to the foundations of the peace settlement.

The narrative follows the German invasion, the making of the Western Front, the failure of offensives, and the defeat of Russia. Sea war, the Balkans, and political reactions at home get their own chapters before the tide turns in 1918. Pollard writes as a professional historian close to the events, and the book served a generation that wanted the war explained whole.
aeroplanes-and-dirigibles-of-war:
Frederick A. Talbot explains, in plain language, how aircraft were being used in the great war then raging in Europe. His preface says the book draws on official reports and men who took part, from British, French, Russian, and German sources. Captive balloons, airships, and aeroplanes all get full treatment.

Chapters cover Germany's airship fleet, scouting from the skies, guiding artillery fire, dropping bombs, armored planes, fights in the air, and guns built to shoot aircraft down. Later chapters take up wireless, naval use, and fleets of the air. The book shows how fast flight changed war while the change was still new.
an-art-lovers-guide-to-the-exposition-ex:
Sheldon Cheney wrote An Art-Lover's Guide to the Exposition as a handbook to the art of the San Francisco exposition, printed at Berkeley in 1915 as its title page shows. He promises two things: to explain the symbolism of the architecture, sculpture, and mural painting, and to point out the special qualities that give each work its appeal.

Chapters walk the grounds court by court — Abundance, the Universe, the Four Seasons, Palms and Flowers. Then take up the Tower of Jewels, the machine and fine arts palaces, and the outdoor sculpture. A closing section guides study inside the fine arts galleries themselves. For a visitor then, or a reader now, it preserves how the fair's art was meant to be read.
ballads-of-peace-in-war:
Michael Earls gathered his verse in Ballads of Peace in War, a book of poems shaped by the First World War and by older American wars. Earls, a Jesuit priest and teacher, writes in ballad stanzas meant to be read aloud. His first poem watches a woman keeping vigil for a sailor at sea. Love and prayer, in his telling, guard the absent man.

Other ballads retell brave deeds and narrow escapes. One poem follows a rider sent to fetch the countersign before a Civil War regiment can advance toward Manassas. Soldiers, mothers, and sweethearts share the pages. Earls favors clear stories, strong rhythm, and Catholic faith over modern experiment. Readers find wartime verse that seeks consolation and courage rather than bitterness about the fighting.
bleek-comparative-grammar:
Wilhelm Bleek published his Comparative Grammar of South African Languages in 1862. The German scholar worked in Cape Town among speakers of many tongues. His book founded the true study of the Bantu language family.

Bleek showed that the Bantu tongues form one great linked family. He worked out their sound laws as Grimm had for Europe's tongues. Noun classes and shared roots lock his case into firm order. The feat ranks among the age's great wins in language science. Scholars still cite his Cape Town work as the field's true start point. Bleek gave African tongues the same respect long given to Europe's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abiathar:
Abiathar was a high priest descended through Achimelech, Achitob, Phinees, Heli, and Ithamar from Aaron, whose name means father of plenty. He alone escaped the slaughter at Nob, fled to David during his banishment, and advised him through his campaigns. With the high priest Sadoc he helped carry the ark to Jerusalem, and he stayed close to David in flight, giving counsel at key moments.

His fortunes turned when he backed Adonias for the throne. Solomon's banishment of him to Anathoth finished the ruin of Ithamar's house foretold in Samuel. The entry tracks his career passage by passage through Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, and points readers to commentaries for the puzzle of 2 Samuel 8:17.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adar:
Adar is four things at once, and this entry separates them. First, a frontier town in Chanaan's south, named in Numbers 34:4 and Joshua 15:3, which has not been identified. Second, it is a king of Edom in Genesis 36:39, called Adad, or Hadad in the Revised Version, at 1 Chronicles 1:50.

Third, Adar is the twelfth month of the Jewish year, matching roughly late February to mid-March. Fourth, Adar is a Chaldean god, whose name appears in the compound Adramelech, meaning Adar is King (2 Kings 17:31). The short entry thus serves as a sorting of one name across place, person, calendar, and god.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-anton-:
Albert Anton von Muchar was an Austrian historian born at Linz in Tyrol in 1781 and dead at Graz in 1849. Descended from the old noble Muchar family, he studied at Graz and joined the Benedictine order at Admont. He was ordained a priest soon after taking his vows in 1808. He later became librarian and keeper of the archives at his monastery, then professor of Greek and eastern languages there.

Muchar's tastes ran to history rather than pure language study. His historical works rest on close reading of original sources in libraries across Austria, Bavaria, and northern Italy. Vienna's Academy of Sciences elected him a member in 1829, and he helped found the Historical Society for Inner Austria. His chief works include Roman Noricum in two volumes and his nine-volume History of the Duchy of Styria, the first four volumes edited by himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avatar:
Avatar comes from the Sanskrit avatara, meaning descent, and names a god's descent to earth in Hindu religion. A portion of the god's essence then takes a coarser form, animal, monster, or man. Vishnu's descents matter most, falling in different ages and measures of his essence. Their number runs from ten to twenty-eight, at last countless.

Any man may be hailed as a more or less perfect avatar of Vishnu. The entry counts that homage to men, above all to sect founders, among Hinduism's worst features. The ten most famous avatars open with the Fish, which saved Manu from the Deluge. Next come the Tortoise, bearing Mount Mandara in the churning of the ocean of milk, and the Boar, lifting the earth from flood. Later avatars adopt the cults of Rama, Krsna, and Buddha, yet their likeness to the Incarnation is most superficial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldachium-of:
A baldachium is a dome-like canopy over the high altar of larger churches. It usually stands on four columns, though sometimes it hangs by chains from the roof. Its late medieval name, baldacchino, comes from Baghdad, source of the precious cloths for such canopies. Earlier it was called ciborium, from Greek kiborion, the lotus seed-pod used as a drinking cup.

It likely arose from the wish to give the plain altar table a dignified architectural setting. By the fourth century it formed the church's architectural center, marking the altar as a throne of honor. Altar curtains hung between its columns, and lamps and crowns hung from its roof. Use ran general until the twelfth century, when the reliquary displaced it, though Italy kept the older form. The most magnificent baldachium is Bernini's in St Peter's, Rome, made for Urban VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baltasar:
Baltasar is the Greek and Latin form of Belshazzar, Hebrew Bel-sarra-usur, meaning 'May Bel protect the king.' Bel was Babylon's chief and titular god. In Daniel chapter five, Baltasar appears as son of Nabuchodonosor and last King of Babylon. While he feasted his nobles, the Medes under Darius invaded the town, and the king was slain.

At the feast he defiled vessels taken from Jerusalem, and his wives and concubines drank from them. A hand then wrote Mane, Thecel, Phares on the wall, which no counsellor or magician could explain. The Queen urged calling Daniel, who read the doom: the kingdom was numbered, the king weighed and found wanting. Its rule would pass to the Medes and the Persians. Herodotus names Labynitus II as Babylon's last king, commonly read as a corruption of Nabonidus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boso-breakspe:
Boso Breakspear, third English cardinal, rose as nephew of Adrian IV and steered the papacy through the schism of 1159. A Benedictine of Saint Albans famed for piety and learning, he wrote lives of eleventh- and twelfth-century popes, including his uncle, and versified saints' lives now in the Cotton manuscripts. Adrian made him cardinal-deacon in December 1155 and camerlengo, and sent him to Portugal.

On Adrian's death, four imperial cardinals chose Octavian as Victor IV, but Boso led twenty-three cardinals into Sant'Angelo on burial day, 5 September 1159, and elected Rolando as Alexander III. Alexander raised him to cardinal-priest in 1163 and took him to Venice for the Peace of 1177 with Frederick. Boso died at Rome about 1181.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buenaventura-:
Buenaventura Sitjar, a Majorcan Franciscan, spent his life at California's San Antonio mission and preserved its Telame language. Born at Porrera, Majorca, on 9 December 1739, he took the habit of Saint Francis in April 1758 and joined the College of San Fernando in Mexico after ordination. Assigned to California in 1770, he landed at San Diego on 21 May 1771.

Present at San Antonio's founding, he served as its first missionary under Junipero Serra until his death on 3 September 1808. By then 3,400 Indians had been baptized there. He mastered Telame, the mission's tongue, and put together a vocabulary with Spanish explanations, issued at New York in 1861. Shorter than Arroyo's Mutsun dictionary, his work gives pronunciation and fuller notes, and he also left a journal of a 1795 exploring expedition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bye-altar: A bye-altar is an altar that ranks below the central or high altar of a church. The name is most often given to altars set in the bays of the nave, the transepts, or other side spaces. Such altars stand apart from the high altar yet within the same church, giving each bay or transept its own place of worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canons-and-ca:
Canons regular are religious clerics who live under a rule while serving the Church's sacramental and pastoral work. The entry sets them apart from monks, for whom clerical status is incidental rather than essential. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, it argues that their order exists precisely for work tied to the divine mysteries. Erasmus himself, a canon regular, called it a middle path between monastic life and the secular clergy.

From origins in the early Church the entry follows their growth, reforms, and congregations across the centuries. It contrasts their choral duties, discipline, dress, and diet with those of Benedictines and Cistercians. English houses get close attention, with dozens founded between the Conquest and the death of Henry II. The account closes with the canonesses regular, the women's branch of the same life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-vica:
The cardinal vicar is the pope's vicar-general for the spiritual government of Rome and its surrounding district, properly called Vicarius Urbis. The entry opens with a critical list of vicars from 1100 to 1600, built from earlier lists by Ponzetti, Moroni, Crostarosa, and Eubel with new manuscript finds. Names before 1100, it warns, must count as uncertain, with Bovo of Tusculum about 1106 the first clearly attested holder.

Until 1260 vicars came from the cardinals, and the first drawn from nearby bishops followed after that date. Later sections set out nomination and oath, authority, the vicegerent, and the organization of the vicariate. Departments covered include ordinations, religious orders, preaching, parochial clergy, the court, and the secretariate. A reform by Pius X, published after the entry's main source, gets a closing note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-cal:
A vast entry on the Christian calendar, the Church's reckoning of time and feasts. It opens with the calendars of Egypt, Babylon, China, India, and the Aztecs, the Celtic calendar stones found at Coligny in 1897, and the verse Fasti of Ovid. It then turns to the Jewish calendar of Leviticus, with lunar months of 29 and 30 days corrected to keep pace with the moon and the sun.

The main body covers the Easter cycle, the Nativity, and saints' days. It goes on to the earliest calendars and feasts of Our Lady and the apostles. Later developments and the modern calendar imposed by authority follow, ending with the churches of the East. Greek movable feasts get close attention, from Sexagesima, the Sunday of abstinence from flesh, to All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost, our Trinity Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
Clerks regular join the religious state's perfection to the priestly office. Essentially clerics, they devote themselves to preaching, sacraments, education of youth, and works of mercy. At the same time they are religious in the strictest sense, professing solemn vows and living community life under a rule approved by the sovereign pontiff. Canon law often uses the term for canons regular, and authors class regular clerks as a branch of the regular canons.

They serve primarily the sacred ministry, not contemplation. They must cultivate the sacred sciences, which monks are not bound to by state of life. As clerics they keep clerical dress distinct from monk's habit and cowl. Their occupations leave them less given to austerity. They differ from friars in being primarily priests, and from canons regular in holding no cathedral churches and giving themselves more to ministry than to choir service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diakovar:
A place and diocesan entry on Diakovar in Slavonia, seat of the united dioceses of Bosnia and Syrmia. In 1900 its 6,824 people were mostly Catholic, about two-thirds Serb and over a quarter German. A Romanesque-Gothic cathedral, finished in 1883 from Rösner's plans by Friedrich Schmidt, runs 256 feet long. Twin towers rise near 276 feet, with a cupola near 203 feet, Seitz frescoes, and an organ of 3,000 pipes.

Roman roots show in the Certissa station on the road from Sissek to Sirmium, lost when peoples moved across Europe in the fourth and fifth centuries. A thirteenth-century gift of Possessio Diaco to the Bishop of Bosnia revived the site, and the see moved to Diakovar in 1246. Seminary, Sisters of Charity house, and episcopal palace complete the picture, with Mariaschnee as the diocese's famed pilgrimage place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dithmar:
Dithmar, also called Thietmar, was bishop of Merseburg and a medieval chronicler. He was born on 25 July 975, son of Count Siegfried of Walbeck and kin to the Saxon emperors. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his schooling at Quedlinburg, Bergen, and Magdeburg. He became provost of Walbeck in 1002, priest in 1003, and fourth bishop of Merseburg in 1009.

As bishop he labored to restore a diocese nearly ruined by his predecessor Giseler, who had chased the archbishopric of Magdeburg. He also defended the freedom of church elections against grasping princes. His chronicle, the great work of his life, remains a chief source for the Saxon age, and the entry lists the editions through which it has reached modern readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-de-sa:
Domingo de Salazar was born at La Bastida on the Ebro in 1512 and died at Madrid in 1594. He joined the Dominicans at San Esteban in Salamanca and was sent to Mexico, where he took a master's degree in theology and a professor's chair. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his wish to preach to the heathen was granted in the province of Guajaca, where he defended Indian rights with zeal.

From Mexico he passed to Florida, laboring for years in toil and privation, then back to Mexico as prior and vice-provincial. After forty years of mission life he was sent to Madrid on order business. The entry closes with his tomb's Latin praise, calling him a father to the poor and poor himself, a fitting epitaph for a defender of the Indians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-double-altar: A double altar carries a double front, allowing Mass to be said on both sides of it at once. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that such altars are often found in churches of religious communities where the choir stands behind the altar. One priest may offer the Holy Sacrifice for the choir community while another offers it for the laity in the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eleazar:
Eleazar is the name of several men in the Bible. This entry starts with the greatest. Eleazar son of Aaron succeeded his father as high priest, wearing Aaron's robes after his death. He stood beside Moses in counting Israel. He helped settle the inheritance claim of the daughters of Salphaad. He shared out the spoils from the Madianites. He heard the plea of Ruben and Gad for land east of the Jordan.

Moses himself presented Joshua, his successor, to Eleazar. Eleazar headed the list of those who divided the land west of the Jordan. He was buried at Gabaath in Mount Ephraim, on ground given to his son Phinees. Down to the Maccabees, the high priests came from his line, apart from the years from Heli to Solomon. The entry also tells of Eleazar Abaron, son of Mathathias, crushed beneath an elephant he had stabbed at Bethzacharam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friar:
Friar names a member of a mendicant order, a begging brotherhood that lives by ministry rather than by cloistered retreat. The word comes from the Latin frater, through French and Middle English forms, and by the late thirteenth century it marked the new orders in English writing. The entry draws the line between friar and monk with care.

For the monk, solitude stands first, and his order may hold property in common. For the friar, public ministry is the heart of life, and his vow of poverty once barred even corporate ownership, so friars lived on free gifts. The Council of Trent later let most mendicant orders hold property together, the Friars Minor and Capuchins alone excepted. Jesuits, though mendicant in spirit, count as clerks regular instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gibraltar:
Gibraltar is a rugged promontory in Andalusia, about six miles round, whose rock rises to 1,396 feet above the strait. The ancient Mount Calpe, paired with Abyla across the water as the Pillars of Hercules, it passed from Phoenicians and Romans to Visigoths and Moors. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces its sieges and its passage from Spain to Britain.

Tarik's Moors built a castle on the rock in 711 and gave it the name Gibel-Tarik, whence Gibraltar. After eight sieges the Spaniards retook it in 1462. In 1704 an English and Dutch force took it during the War of the Spanish Succession. The Treaty of Utrecht made it British in 1713. Its fourteenth and last siege ran from July 1779 for three years, seven months, and twelve days, and failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamar:
Norway's medieval diocese of Hamar covered Hedemarken and Christians Amt, formed in 1152 from Oslo when Arnold, former Bishop of Gardar in Greenland, became its first bishop. He began Christ Church cathedral, finished about the time of Bishop Paul in the mid-thirteenth century. The see grew a chapter of ten canons, a school, a Dominican priory, and a monastery.

Later bishops include Thorfinn, exiled to Flanders where he died, Jörund, moved to Trondhjem, and a provincial council held in 1380. Mogens, the last Catholic bishop, ruled from 1513 to 1537 before a Danish noble seized him in his castle and carried him to Antvorskov. There he lived mildly treated until his death in 1542.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-frie:
Henry of Friemar, a German theologian born at Friemar near Gotha toward the end of the thirteenth century, entered the Augustinian Hermits young and was posted to the University of Paris. There he became master of sacred theology and taught until 1318. That year he became regent of studies at St. Thomas's monastery in Prague and examiner for Germany, later provincial for Thuringia and Saxony. He probably died at Erfurt about 1355.

His printed works show wide range. They include a collection of sermons on the saints, a treatise on the fourfold instinct, divine, angelic, diabolic, and human, and additions to the Sentences. A work on spirits and their discernment, a tract on the conception of the Blessed Virgin, and a history of the origins of the Augustinian Hermits complete the list. His writings circulated in print from Cologne to Parma and Louvain across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-kalk:
Henry of Kalkar, a Carthusian writer born at Kalkar in Cleves in 1328, studied at Cologne and Paris. He became Master of Arts in 1357, procurator of the German nation, and professor of theology. After canonries at Kaiserswerth and Cologne he withdrew in 1365 to Cologne's Charterhouse. He rose to prior of Arnheim, Ruremonde, Cologne, and Strasburg, and served twenty years as visitor amid the Great Schism. Relieved of office in 1396, he lived in prayer at Cologne until his death in 1408.

Kalkar was celebrated as reformer as well as writer: at Arnheim he drew Gerard Groote into the Charterhouse. His writings influenced the school of Deventer and Windesheim, organizing the Catholic Renaissance that found expression at Trent. Many wrongly credited him with the Rosary and the Imitation, yet the Exercitatorium Monachale is certainly his, inspiring Thomas à Kempis and supplying ideas for Ignatius's Exercises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-of-fr:
Two German works on mysticism carry the name Hermann of Fritzlar, and this entry sorts out what belongs to him and what does not. The first, Das Heiligenleben, is a set of ninety-one short sermons on saints' lives written between 1343 and 1349. It mixes plain teaching with mystical thought on union with God and the birth of Christ in the soul. Long credited to Hermann, it was in fact compiled at his request by the Dominican preacher Gisiler of Slatheim.

The second work, Blume der Schauung, or Flower of Contemplation, survives in a Nuremberg manuscript. It gathers loosely linked questions on the contemplative life and its models. Readers interested in fourteenth-century German mysticism find here a careful untangling of authorship, sources, and the blend of first- and third-person voice in the sermons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-high-altar:
The high altar is the chief altar in a church, raised on an elevated plane in the sanctuary so that all the faithful can see it at once. It symbolizes Christ, and it serves as the banquet table on which Christ offers himself through the priest's hands to the Eternal Father. A sacrifice supposes both priest and altar, and the Acts of the Apostles shows the faithful sharing in the prayers and partaking of the victim.

In early days the altar usually stood in a chapel at the head of the church, facing east, following the tradition that the faithful pray toward the east. If a church could not be built that way, the altar stood opposite the chief doorway. Olden churches had but one altar, and the entry traces how the high altar's place, form, and meaning developed from those beginnings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-th:
The Christian altar is an elevated, table-like surface for offering the Sacrifice of the Mass. Its earliest scriptural reference is in St. Paul, who sets the table of the Lord, trapeza Kyriou, against the table of devils, or pagan altars. Greek Fathers kept trapeza as their favourite term, while Hebrews calls the altar thysiasterion, a word used by Ignatius and later Fathers for the Christian altar.

Christians of the first age carefully avoided bomos, with its pagan associations, until Synesius used it in the early fifth century. Latin writers used altare, mensa, ara, and altarium, though ara more often meant a pagan altar. The entry traces names, forms, and fittings from those early tables through great church altars, their columns, and the iconostasis of the Greek church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-issachar:

Scripture tells little of him beyond his four sons at the descent into Egypt. Second, the tribe descended from him, about which knowledge stays thin. In the wilderness march the tribe camped east of the tabernacle with Judah and Zebulun.

At Sinai's first census Issachar counted 54,400 warriors, and 64,300 at the second census, figures the entry quotes from Numbers. After entering western Palestine the tribe settled its allotted land, its later story fading from the record. Readers get a careful distinction: a patriarch known mainly as a name, and a tribe known mainly through census rolls and camp order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-goar:

Though lector of philosophy and theology, he devoted himself to Greek study. His superiors sent him to the East to serve Rome through knowledge of Greek church documents and positive theology.

He lived at Chios as missionary apostolic and prior of St Sebastian convent. He used travel to observe rites, meet Orthodox scholars, and study Catholic-Orthodox points at issue. About 1640 he returned to Rome bearing many manuscripts, some valuable. Thereafter he corresponded with the most learned Greeks of his day. The entry presents a scholar-diplomat bridging Latin and Greek Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jewish-calend:
The Jewish Calendar entry explains how Israel has reckoned time from earliest days to the present. The day runs sunset to sunset, or to the first three stars, and before exile daylight was split only into morning, midday, and evening. Babylon brought twelve varying hours, the first near six in the morning and the sixth ending at noon.

Nights were first kept in three watches, to midnight, to cock-crow near three, and to dawn. Weeks count seven numbered days, the seventh called Sabbath, a name also used for the week itself, while Friday bears the title eve of Sabbath or day of preparation. Months, feasts, and leap years complete a system binding worship to seasons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:

His chief task was continuing Count Leopold Stolberg's History of the Religion of Jesus Christ. He wrote its forty-fifth through fifty-fourth volumes. The entry judges that work below his predecessor's standard. He also wrote two volumes on the disputes between Paolo Sarpi and Pallavicini. He added a monograph on Pope Innocent III, a five-volume survey of Catholic pulpit orators in Germany, and many articles for Herder's church lexicon.

Born at Strasbourg in 1760 and ordained in 1783, he stayed in the city through the Terror in disguise, giving the sacraments in secret. After Robespierre's fall he preached across Strasbourg, and Napoleon named him Bishop of Mainz in 1802.

Colmar found his cathedral profaned and his diocese ruined by war and confiscation. He rebuilt and reconsecrated the cathedral, saved Speyer's from demolition, opened a seminary in 1804, and visited every parish and school. During the epidemic of 1813 and 1814 he served the sick himself. He died at Mainz in 1818.
